source.title: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Deep Models: Effective Dimensionality Revisited
source.authors: Wesley J. Maddox; Gregory W. Benton; A. Wilson

record.tranche_reason: The paper varies network width and depth and measures test loss/error and generalization gaps, and compares generalization measures using a different measure from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports width/depth sweeps and correlations of effective dimensionality and alternative measures with generalization. It also cites prior findings, which are not extracted as rows. Values in Figures 1, 2, 7, and 9 are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study tests width-dependent generalization and magnitude-aware perturbation measures in new architectures and datasets. Post-interpolation double descent does not itself challenge V2; the supplementary width experiment explicitly reports a plateau after training loss reaches zero.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly captures the authors' conclusion: effective dimensionality tracks generalization among models with comparable training loss and helps explain double descent and width-depth tradeoffs. Their claim of favorable overall comparison should not be restated as uniformly best correlation: log path-norm exceeds effective dimensionality in several table entries.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains width/depth sweeps with SGD, weight decay, and augmentation; it measures test loss/error and generalization correlations rather than the exact V2 setup or magnitude-aware sharpness protocol in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Width and depth change test performance; 20% label corruption yields double descent in test error, which the paper says is not clearly present in test error without corruption. The PAC-Bayes measure is sensitive to model size and perturbation scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective dimensionality correlates with test performance and generalization gaps, and distinguishes width-depth tradeoffs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Among models with comparable low training loss and fixed parameterization, lower Hessian effective dimensionality is associated with better generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Magnitude-aware PAC-Bayes sharpness correlates positively with test loss and test error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Magnitude-aware random-perturbation sharpness tracks held-out performance across these architecture sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: Perturbations in low-curvature subspaces largely preserve predictions, including over 99% classification agreement on CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many low-curvature parameter directions produce little functional diversity near a trained solution.

record.problems: The neural-network Hessian effective dimensionality uses only about 100 leading eigenvalues, and the authors state estimates are biased by omitting small eigenvalues. Several sweep results are conveyed in figures without exact numerical values. Reported associations are correlations.
record.rows_left_out: None of the extracted results exceeded the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label training, memorization capacity, and chance-level random-label test accuracy.

The original one-hidden-layer ReLU, MNIST/downsampled CIFAR-10, convergence-without-explicit-regularization recipe. The clean-label ResNet loss sweep does not establish the specified test-error trend.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, learned local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Controlled optimizer comparisons and tuning, switching, or decoupled-weight-decay interventions.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations under controlled epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.

The original CIFAR-10/SVHN setting without augmentation, magnitude-aware sharpness beyond the expected-random-perturbation implementation, margin-based comparisons, and rank-based association statistics; this study reports Pearson correlations.
Memorization-based example removal versus equally sized random removal.

missing.what: Post-interpolation width plateau for three-hidden-layer ELU networks on two spirals; Figure A.5 reports constant test performance, with 25 repetitions and two-standard-deviation shading.
Log path-norm generalization-gap correlations: 0.9257 for the clean ResNet18 width sweep and 0.9602 for the CNN width-depth sweep. Raw path-norm correlations are 0.5259 and 0.7511, respectively.

For ResNet18s with 20% corruption and training loss below 0.1, gap correlations are 0.7956 for magnitude-aware PAC-Bayes, 0.8578 for effective dimensionality, 0.7937 for path-norm, and 0.9836 for log path-norm.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the tested versions. Training uses augmentation and weight decay; disabling augmentation for Hessian computation does not make training an unaugmented experiment. Pearson correlation measures association, not ranking accuracy or causation. Figure-only results can establish a direction when the text explicitly states it, but exact effect sizes remain unavailable.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization and chance-level test performance.
One-hidden-layer ReLU networks, MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10, and the exact no-explicit-regularization recipe.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the causal role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and their tuning conditions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions and their interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.

The specific convolutional family and datasets CIFAR-10 and SVHN without augmentation; the paper tests CIFAR-100. Its comparison includes magnitude-aware PAC-Bayes sharpness, but the broader version’s tested-measure set is not fully reproduced.
Removing memorized examples and comparing with random-example removal.
